title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
The MOFA2 Idea
Omics layer 1: RNA-seq    (n_samples × n_genes)
Omics layer 2: Methylation (n_samples × n_CpGs)
Omics layer 3: Metabolomics (n_samples × n_metabolites)
         ↓
MOFA2: find latent factors that explain variance ACROSS layers

Factor 1 → driven by cell cycle genes + methylation changes
Factor 2 → driven by immune activity in RNA + microbiome
Factor 3 → driven by metabolic genes + metabolites

Each factor = a biological axis of variation shared across omics layers

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
Building a MOFA2 Model

library(MOFA2)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Load each omics layer (same samples, different features)
rna   <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "rna_matrix.rds"))     # genes × samples
meth  <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "meth_matrix.rds"))    # CpGs × samples
micro <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "microbiome_matrix.rds")) # taxa × samples

# Create MOFA object
mofa <- create_mofa(list(
  RNA          = rna,
  Methylation  = meth,
  Microbiome   = micro
))

# Visualize data overview
plot_data_overview(mofa)

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
DIABLO — Multi-block Discriminant Analysis
Goal: find a combination of features across omics layers
      that best discriminates between groups (e.g., responder vs. non-responder)

Input:
  X = list of omics matrices (RNA, methylation, proteomics)
  Y = outcome variable (factor: responder / non-responder)

Output:
  - Selected features per layer
  - Correlation structure between layers
  - Classification model

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
Running DIABLO

library(mixOmics)

# Input data
X <- list(
  RNA    = t(rna_filtered),      # samples × features
  Methyl = t(meth_filtered),
  Micro  = t(micro_filtered)
)
Y <- factor(sample_metadata$response)   # "Responder" / "Non-responder"

# Design matrix — how correlated should layers be?
# 1 = maximize inter-layer correlation
# 0 = maximize discrimination only
design <- matrix(0.1,
                  ncol = length(X),
                  nrow = length(X),
                  dimnames = list(names(X), names(X)))
diag(design) <- 0

# Initial DIABLO run
diablo <- block.splsda(X, Y,
                        ncomp  = 5,
                        design = design)

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
Tuning & Final Model

# Tune number of features to select per layer
set.seed(42)
perf_diablo <- perf(diablo,
                     validation    = "Mfold",
                     folds         = 5,
                     nrepeat       = 10,
                     dist          = "centroids.dist")

# Optimal number of components
plot(perf_diablo)
ncomp_opt <- perf_diablo$choice.ncomp$WeightedVote["Overall.BER",
                                                     "centroids.dist"]

# Tune number of features
test_keepX <- list(RNA    = c(5, 10, 15, 20),
                   Methyl = c(5, 10, 15),
                   Micro  = c(3, 5, 10))

tune_diablo <- tune.block.splsda(X, Y,
                                  ncomp      = ncomp_opt,
                                  test.keepX = test_keepX,
                                  design     = design,
                                  validation = "Mfold",
                                  folds      = 5,
                                  nrepeat    = 10)

# Final model
final_diablo <- block.splsda(X, Y,
                              ncomp    = ncomp_opt,
                              keepX    = tune_diablo$choice.keepX,
                              design   = design)

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
DIABLO Visualizations

# Circos plot — cross-layer correlations of selected features
circosPlot(final_diablo,
           cutoff        = 0.7,
           line          = TRUE,
           color.blocks  = c("#1D9E75", "#534AB7", "#D85A30"),
           color.cor     = c("#D85A30", "#1D9E75"))

# Sample plot
plotDiablo(final_diablo, ncomp = 1)

# Heatmap of selected features
cimDiablo(final_diablo,
          color.blocks = c("#1D9E75", "#534AB7", "#D85A30"),
          comp         = 1,
          margin       = c(8, 20),
          legend.position = "topright")

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
section: The Problem: GWAS Hit → Causal Gene
text:
The Problem: GWAS Hit → Causal Gene
A GWAS locus typically contains: - 1 lead SNP - Dozens of correlated SNPs in LD - Multiple nearby genes
Which gene is the actual effector?
Evidence layers for gene prioritization:
├── Positional     → nearest gene
├── eQTL           → gene whose expression is controlled by the SNP
├── Chromatin      → SNP overlaps enhancer contacting gene X (Hi-C)
├── Epigenomic     → SNP in cell-type-specific open chromatin
├── scRNA-seq      → gene expressed in disease-relevant cell type
└── Multi-omics    → gene appears across multiple evidence layers

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
H-MAGMA — Cell-Type-Specific Prioritization

# H-MAGMA: uses Hi-C contacts from specific cell types
# to map SNPs to genes via chromatin interactions

# Pre-computed H-MAGMA results for different tissues
# (neurons, cardiomyocytes, immune cells, etc.)

hmagma_neuron <- read_tsv(
  here("data", "processed", "hmagma_adult_brain.genes.out")
) |> arrange(P)

hmagma_immune <- read_tsv(
  here("data", "processed", "hmagma_immune.genes.out")
) |> arrange(P)

# Compare: different genes prioritized in neurons vs. immune cells
# for same GWAS → cell-type specificity of disease mechanism
inner_join(
  hmagma_neuron  |> select(GENE, P_neuron  = P),
  hmagma_immune  |> select(GENE, P_immune  = P)
) |>
  filter(P_neuron < 0.05 | P_immune < 0.05) |>
  mutate(cell_type_specific = case_when(
    P_neuron < 0.05 & P_immune > 0.05 ~ "Neuron-specific",
    P_immune < 0.05 & P_neuron > 0.05 ~ "Immune-specific",
    TRUE ~ "Both"
  ))

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
You Are Not Alone

~38 trillion microbial cells in/on the human body (~1:1 with human cells)
~3.3 million microbial genes (vs. ~20,000 human protein-coding genes)
99% of the microbiome is in the gut
Collectively called the gut microbiome or gut flora


Clinically relevant in: IBD, IBS, colorectal cancer, T2D, obesity, cardiovascular disease,
mental health (gut–brain axis), autoimmune disease, drug metabolism,
immunotherapy response

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
section: Why This Matters for Drug Response
text:
Why This Matters for Drug Response

Irinotecan (CPT-11) — gut bacteria reactivate the drug in the colon → diarrhea
Checkpoint inhibitors — Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Akkermansia associated with response
Metformin — microbiome mediates glycemic effects
Antibiotics → dysbiosis → C. difficile → CDI








The gut–immunotherapy connection


Patients with high Akkermansia muciniphila abundance respond significantly better to anti-PD1 therapy.
This has been replicated in multiple cohorts across multiple tumor types.

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Why 16S rRNA?
16S rRNA gene:
├── Conserved regions  → universal PCR primers
└── Variable regions   → species identification
    (V1-V2, V3-V4, V4 most common)

Workflow:
Stool/swab DNA → PCR amplify V3-V4 → Sequence → Assign taxonomy

Pros: Cheap (~$50/sample), easy, large reference databases
Cons: Amplification bias, ~genus level resolution, no functional info
→ For functional metagenomics: Whole Metagenome Shotgun (WMS) — next week (W7)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
ASV vs. OTU — Modern Standard
OTU (Operational Taxonomic Unit) — old approach: - Cluster reads at 97% similarity → OTU table - Information loss, not reproducible
ASV (Amplicon Sequence Variant) — current standard (DADA2): - Exact sequence variants, corrected for sequencing errors - Reproducible across studies - Higher resolution (can distinguish strains)


Always use DADA2 / ASVs for new studies.
QIIME2 wraps DADA2 — both acceptable.

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Analysis Workflow
Raw paired-end FASTQ (R1 + R2)
    │
    ├── 1. Quality inspection   → plotQualityProfile()
    ├── 2. Filtering & trimming → filterAndTrim()
    ├── 3. Error learning       → learnErrors()
    ├── 4. Denoising (DADA2)   → dada()
    ├── 5. Merging pairs        → mergePairs()
    ├── 6. Chimera removal      → removeBimeraDenovo()
    ├── 7. Taxonomy assignment  → assignTaxonomy() → SILVA
    └── 8. Phyloseq object      → diversity, composition analysis

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 1: Quality Profiles

library(dada2)
library(here)

# List raw FASTQ files
fnFs <- sort(list.files(here("data", "raw", "fastq"),
                         pattern = "_R1_001.fastq.gz",
                         full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(here("data", "raw", "fastq"),
                         pattern = "_R2_001.fastq.gz",
                         full.names = TRUE))

sample_names <- sub("_R1_001.fastq.gz", "",
                    basename(fnFs))

# Visualize quality profiles
plotQualityProfile(fnFs[1:2])   # forward reads
plotQualityProfile(fnRs[1:2])   # reverse reads
# Quality usually drops at end of reads — decide truncation point

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 2: Filter & Trim

# Output paths
filtFs <- file.path(here("data", "processed", "filtered"),
                    paste0(sample_names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(here("data", "processed", "filtered"),
                    paste0(sample_names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))

# Filter — adjust truncLen based on quality profile
out <- filterAndTrim(
  fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs,
  truncLen    = c(240, 200),   # forward, reverse
  maxN        = 0,             # no Ns allowed
  maxEE       = c(2, 2),       # max expected errors
  truncQ      = 2,
  rm.phix     = TRUE,
  compress    = TRUE,
  multithread = TRUE
)

head(out)
# Check: >70% reads should pass filter

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 3–4: Learn Errors & Denoise

# Learn error rates (takes ~10 min on 20 samples)
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread = TRUE)
errR <- learnErrors(filtRs, multithread = TRUE)

# Visualize error model — points should follow the line
plotErrors(errF, nominalQ = TRUE)

# DADA2 denoising — the core step
dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err = errF, multithread = TRUE,
               pool = "pseudo")   # pool for rare ASVs
dadaRs <- dada(filtRs, err = errR, multithread = TRUE,
               pool = "pseudo")

dadaFs[[1]]
# dada-class: 128 sample sequences

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
section: Step 5–7: Merge, Remove Chimeras, Assign Taxonomy
text:
Step 5–7: Merge, Remove Chimeras, Assign Taxonomy

# Merge paired reads
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs,
                      dadaRs, filtRs,
                      verbose = TRUE)

# Make sequence table
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)

# Inspect ASV length distribution — should center on ~253 bp (V3-V4)
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab)))

# Remove chimeras
seqtab_nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab,
                                    method     = "consensus",
                                    multithread = TRUE,
                                    verbose    = TRUE)

# Fraction of reads retained
sum(seqtab_nochim) / sum(seqtab)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Taxonomy Assignment

# SILVA database (download v138.1 from https://zenodo.org/record/4587955)
taxa <- assignTaxonomy(
  seqtab_nochim,
  here("data", "raw", "silva_nr99_v138.1_train_set.fa.gz"),
  multithread = TRUE
)

# Add species-level assignment
taxa <- addSpecies(
  taxa,
  here("data", "raw", "silva_species_assignment_v138.1.fa.gz")
)

# Preview
taxa_df <- as.data.frame(taxa)
head(taxa_df)
# Kingdom  Phylum          Class     Order      Family     Genus   Species
# Bacteria Bacteroidota    ...

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Track Reads Through Pipeline

getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))

track <- cbind(
  out,
  sapply(dadaFs, getN),
  sapply(dadaRs, getN),
  sapply(mergers, getN),
  rowSums(seqtab_nochim)
)

colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF",
                      "denoisedR", "merged", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample_names

head(track)
# Should retain >70% from input to nonchim
# Large drops at merge → primer trimming needed
# Large drops at chimera → primer length issues

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Building the phyloseq Object

library(phyloseq)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Load sample metadata
metadata <- read_tsv(here("data", "raw", "sample_metadata.tsv")) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Build phyloseq object
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(seqtab_nochim, taxa_are_rows = FALSE),
  sample_data(metadata),
  tax_table(taxa)
)

# Rename ASVs to short names
dna <- Biostrings::DNAStringSet(taxa_names(ps))
names(dna) <- paste0("ASV", seq(ntaxa(ps)))
taxa_names(ps) <- names(dna)

ps

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Alpha Diversity — Within-Sample Diversity

# Rarefy to equal depth first
ps_rare <- rarefy_even_depth(ps,
                              sample.size = min(sample_sums(ps)),
                              rngseed     = 42)

# Alpha diversity metrics
alpha_div <- estimate_richness(ps_rare,
                                measures = c("Observed",
                                             "Shannon",
                                             "Simpson",
                                             "Chao1"))

alpha_div <- alpha_div |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  left_join(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame") |>
            rownames_to_column("sample_id"))

# Compare between groups
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = Group, y = Shannon, fill = Group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  stat_compare_means() +
  labs(title = "Shannon diversity by group") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Beta Diversity — Between-Sample Diversity

library(vegan)

# Bray-Curtis dissimilarity — most common for microbiome
bray_dist <- distance(ps_rare, method = "bray")

# PCoA ordination
ord_pcoa <- ordinate(ps_rare, method = "PCoA",
                      distance = bray_dist)

# Plot
plot_ordination(ps_rare, ord_pcoa,
                color = "Group",
                shape = "Group") +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse() +
  labs(title = "PCoA — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity") +
  theme_minimal()

# PERMANOVA — is the group difference significant?
adonis2(bray_dist ~ Group + age + sex,
        data = as(sample_data(ps_rare), "data.frame"),
        permutations = 999)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
From W2:


GWAS finds variants at p < 5×10⁻⁸
But most complex diseases are polygenic / omnigenic — thousands of variants
Each with a tiny effect (OR ≈ 1.02–1.15)
No single variant is clinically useful alone




A PRS aggregates the effects of (up to) millions of SNPs into one number per person.






For person i, sum the GWAS effect size \(\hat\beta_j\) × allele dosage \(G_{ij}\) over all variants j:
\[\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \hat\beta_j \, G_{ij}\]
Person A:
  rs1001  risk allele × 0.03
+ rs2045  risk allele × 0.02
+ rs8821  non-risk    × 0.00
+ ... (thousands–millions more)
─────────────────────────────────
= PRS 1.42  → top 20% of population → ~3× risk

Crucially, variants below genome-wide significance still carry real signal — PRS deliberately includes them [Reay & Cairns 2021].







W2’s omnigenic model: thousands of variants each nudge the trait
Single hits capture a sliver of heritability; aggregation captures much more
PRS is the clinical pay-off of polygenicity — one saliva sample → lifetime genetic predisposition








Note



A PRS is a risk indicator, not a diagnosis. It shifts a probability; it does not determine an outcome.








Coronary artery disease — flags high-risk people for earlier statins
Breast cancer — stratifies risk beyond BRCA1/2; guides screening intensity
Type 2 diabetes — PRS + lifestyle → targeted prevention
Atrial fibrillation — predicts incident AF beyond clinical scores
Prostate / colorectal cancer — screening intensity









TipThe clinician’s question



PRS adds information on top of age, BMI, family history, biomarkers. The bar is always: does it change management?

title: W3. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 1: C+T (Clumping and Thresholding)
The simplest approach:
1. Clumping: keep only one SNP per LD block
   (remove correlated SNPs → independent signals only)

2. Thresholding: keep SNPs below a p-value cutoff
   (e.g., p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 5×10⁻⁸)

3. PRS = Σ (effect size × allele count)

library(bigsnpr)

# C+T with PRSice2 (via system call) or bigsnpr
obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here("data", "raw", "target.rds"))
G <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes

# Clumping
ind.keep <- snp_clumping(
  G,
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  S         = abs(sumstats$Z),     # use Z-score for clumping
  thr.r2    = 0.1,
  size      = 500
)

title: W3. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 2: LDpred2 — The Current Standard
Accounts for LD structure more accurately using a Bayesian framework:

library(bigsnpr)

# Step 1: Match summary stats to target genotypes
sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, obj.bigsnp$map)

# Step 2: Compute LD reference matrix
POS2 <- snp_asGeneticPos(
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  dir       = here("data", "raw", "genetic_maps")
)

corr <- snp_cor(G, ind.col = sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`,
                infos.pos = POS2, size = 3 / 1000)

# Step 3: LDpred2-auto (no tuning needed)
ldsc <- with(sumstats,
             snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                      chi2  = (beta / beta_se)^2,
                      sample_size = n_eff))

h2_est <- ldsc[["h2"]]

multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(
  corr, sumstats, h2_init = h2_est,
  vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, length.out = 30),
  burn_in = 500, num_iter = 500, report_step = 20
)

# Command-line tool, called from R
system(paste(
  "PRSice",
  "--base",          here::here("data", "raw", "sumstats.txt"),
  "--target",        here::here("data", "raw", "target_plink"),
  "--binary-target", "T",
  "--pheno",         here::here("data", "raw", "phenotype.txt"),

text:

Method
Pros
Cons




C+T
Fast, interpretable
Loses information, arbitrary threshold


LDpred2

text:
Key Performance Metrics

library(tidyverse)

# Load PRS scores + phenotype
prs_data <- read_tsv(here("results", "prsice_output.best")) |>
  left_join(phenotype, by = "IID")

# Nagelkerke R² — variance explained by PRS
library(DescTools)

# Null model (covariates only)
null_model <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5,
                  data   = prs_data,
                  family = binomial)

# Full model (covariates + PRS)
full_model <- glm(disease ~ PRS + age + sex + PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5,
                  data   = prs_data,
                  family = binomial)

r2_prs <- PseudoR2(full_model, "Nagelkerke") -
          PseudoR2(null_model, "Nagelkerke")
cat("R² explained by PRS:", round(r2_prs, 4), "\n")

title: W3. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
AUC and Discrimination

library(pROC)

# ROC curve — does PRS improve discrimination?
roc_null <- roc(prs_data$disease,
                predict(null_model, type = "response"))

roc_full <- roc(prs_data$disease,
                predict(full_model, type = "response"))

# Compare AUCs
roc.test(roc_null, roc_full)

# Plot
ggroc(list(Clinical = roc_null,
           `Clinical + PRS` = roc_full)) +
  labs(title = "ROC: Does PRS improve prediction?",
       color  = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()

title: W3. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Quantile Plot — Clinical Interpretation

# Divide PRS into deciles
prs_data <- prs_data |>
  mutate(prs_decile = ntile(PRS, 10))

# Odds ratio per decile vs. middle decile (reference)
or_by_decile <- prs_data |>
  group_by(prs_decile) |>
  summarise(
    n_cases    = sum(disease == 1),
    n_controls = sum(disease == 0)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    OR = (n_cases / n_controls) /
         (n_cases[prs_decile == 5] / n_controls[prs_decile == 5])
  )

ggplot(or_by_decile, aes(prs_decile, OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "PRS decile",
       y = "Odds Ratio vs. middle decile",
       title = "Disease risk by PRS decile") +
  theme_minimal()

section: PRS in Diverse Populations — A Real Problem
text:
PRS in Diverse Populations — A Real Problem


Most GWAS (and therefore PRS) are trained on European-ancestry individuals
PRS built on European GWAS performs 4–5× worse in African-ancestry populations
Applying biased PRS clinically could widen health disparities
Active research: PRS-CSx, multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis









ImportantFor Korean patients



Korean-specific GWAS (KoGES, KCHIP, TOPMed Korean) exist for major diseases.
Always check whether the base GWAS matches your target population’s ancestry.

title: W3. Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
What PRS Cannot Do


Causality — high PRS ≠ will develop disease
Rare variants — PRS misses high-penetrance rare variants (BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome)
Gene–environment interaction — genetic risk can be modified by lifestyle
Replace clinical judgment — PRS is one input, not a diagnosis

  mutate(PRS = prs_scores)

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Beyond the DNA Sequence
Same genome. Different cell types. Different functions.
Neuron  ─── DNA ──→  expresses NEFL, SNAP25, SYP
Hepatocyte ─ DNA ──→  expresses ALB, CYP3A4, F2
T cell  ─── DNA ──→  expresses CD3E, CD8A, GZMB

The genome is the same. The epigenome is different.
Epigenomics studies the regulatory layer on top of the DNA sequence: - DNA methylation - Histone modifications - Chromatin accessibility (W5) - 3D genome organization (W5)

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Why Epigenomics for Clinicians?

Cancer — global hypomethylation + gene-specific hypermethylation → tumor suppressor silencing
Aging — epigenetic clocks predict biological age, mortality, disease risk
Drug response — methylation status of promoters predicts chemotherapy sensitivity
Developmental disorders — imprinting diseases (Prader-Willi, Angelman)
Liquid biopsy — cell-free DNA methylation → tissue of origin for cancer detection

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
The Biology
CpG dinucleotide:  5'─C─G─3'
                   3'─G─C─5'

Methylation:   5'─[m]C─G─3'   (5-methylcytosine)

Maintained by: DNMT1 (maintenance methyltransferase)
Written by:    DNMT3A / DNMT3B (de novo)
Erased by:     TET enzymes (oxidation → demethylation)

Effect on gene expression: - Promoter methylation → gene silencing - Gene body methylation → associated with active transcription (context-dependent) - Enhancer methylation → reduced enhancer activity

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
CpG Islands, Shores, and Shelves
                shore    CGI      shore
──────────────[====][===========][====]──────────────
              shelf                     shelf

CpG Island (CGI): high CpG density, usually unmethylated in normal tissue
Shore (0–2 kb):   variable methylation, most disease-relevant
Shelf (2–4 kb):   lower CpG density
Open sea:         remaining genome






Clinically important


Most cancer-associated methylation changes happen at CGI shores, not the islands themselves.

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Overview
Raw IDAT files (Illumina array)
    │
    ├── 1. Load & QC          → minfi / ChAMP
    ├── 2. Normalization       → BMIQ / Noob
    ├── 3. Filtering           → remove SNP-associated, cross-reactive probes
    ├── 4. DMP analysis        → differentially methylated positions
    ├── 5. DMR analysis        → differentially methylated regions
    ├── 6. Functional annotation → gene, CGI context
    └── 7. Epigenetic clock    → biological age estimation

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 1: Load IDAT Files

library(minfi)
library(here)

# Read sample sheet
targets <- read.metharray.sheet(here("data", "raw", "methylation"),
                                 pattern = "SampleSheet.csv")

# Load raw IDAT files
rgSet <- read.metharray.exp(targets = targets,
                             verbose  = TRUE)
rgSet

# Check: should see ~935,000 probes (EPIC) or ~485,000 (450K)

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 2: QC

# QC report
qcReport(rgSet,
         sampNames = targets$Sample_Name,
         sampGroups = targets$Sample_Group,
         pdf       = here("results", "qc_report.pdf"))

# Detection p-values — probes with p > 0.01 are unreliable
detP <- detectionP(rgSet)
failed <- detP > 0.01
cat("Failed probes per sample:\n")
colSums(failed)

# Remove samples with > 1% failed probes
keep <- colMeans(failed) < 0.01
rgSet <- rgSet[, keep]
cat("Samples remaining:", ncol(rgSet), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 3: Normalization

# Noob + BMIQ normalization — recommended for EPIC
mSet <- preprocessNoob(rgSet)
mSet <- BMIQ(mSet)   # within-sample normalization

# Extract beta values (0–1, proportion methylated)
beta <- getBeta(mSet)

# Extract M-values (logit of beta, better for statistics)
mval <- getM(mSet)

# Beta values for visualization, M-values for statistical testing
cat("Beta matrix:", nrow(beta), "probes ×", ncol(beta), "samples\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 4: Probe Filtering

library(maxprobes)   # cross-reactive probes list

# Remove probes that:
# 1. Failed QC in any sample
keep_probes <- rowSums(detP > 0.01) == 0

# 2. Are on sex chromosomes (if not studying sex differences)
annot <- getAnnotation(mSet)
keep_probes <- keep_probes & !(annot$chr %in% c("chrX", "chrY"))

# 3. Contain known SNPs at CpG site
keep_probes <- keep_probes & is.na(annot$Probe_maf)

# 4. Are known cross-reactive
xreact <- xreactive_probes(array_type = "EPIC")
keep_probes <- keep_probes & !(rownames(mSet) %in% xreact)

mSet_filtered <- mSet[keep_probes, ]
cat("Probes after filtering:", nrow(mSet_filtered), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 5: Differential Methylation — DMPs

library(limma)

# Design matrix — adjust for age, sex, cell type composition
design <- model.matrix(
  ~ Group + age + sex + CD8T + CD4T + NK + Bcell + Mono + Gran,
  data = targets
)

# Fit linear model on M-values
fit <- lmFit(mval[keep_probes, ], design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)

# Extract DMPs
dmps <- topTable(fit,
                 coef    = "GroupCase",
                 number  = Inf,
                 sort.by = "p") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "probe")

# Significant DMPs
sig_dmps <- dmps |>
  filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05, abs(logFC) > 0.1)

cat("Significant DMPs:", nrow(sig_dmps), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 6: Differential Methylation — DMRs

library(DMRcate)

# DMR analysis — finds regions of co-methylated probes
myannotation <- cpg.annotate(
  object       = mval,
  datatype     = "array",
  what         = "M",
  analysis.type = "differential",
  design       = design,
  coef         = "GroupCase",
  arraytype    = "EPIC"
)

# Find DMRs
dmrcoutput <- dmrcate(myannotation,
                      lambda   = 1000,
                      C        = 2)

dmrs <- extractRanges(dmrcoutput, genome = "hg19")
dmrs

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 7: Visualization

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Volcano plot of DMPs
ggplot(dmps, aes(x = logFC, y = -log10(adj.P.Val))) +
  geom_point(aes(color = abs(logFC) > 0.1 & adj.P.Val < 0.05),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray70", "#D85A30")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.1, 0.1), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x     = "Δβ (M-value logFC)",
       y     = "-log10(adj. p-value)",
       title = "Differentially Methylated Positions",
       color = "Significant") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Cell Type Deconvolution — Critical Confounder

library(minfi)

# Whole blood methylation is a mixture of cell types
# Must estimate and correct for cell type composition

cell_counts <- estimateCellCounts2(
  rgSet,
  referencePlatform = "IlluminaHumanMethylationEPIC",
  returnAll         = FALSE
)

# Cell type proportions
head(cell_counts)
# CD8T  CD4T  NK  Bcell  Mono  Gran

# Visualize
cell_counts |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "sample") |>
  pivot_longer(-sample, names_to = "cell_type", values_to = "proportion") |>
  ggplot(aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Estimated blood cell type composition")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Biological Age vs. Chronological Age

Horvath clock (2013) — multi-tissue, 353 CpGs → predicts chronological age
Hannum clock (2013) — blood-specific, 71 CpGs
PhenoAge (2018) — predicts mortality, not just age
GrimAge (2019) — predicts time-to-death and disease onset
DunedinPACE (2022) — pace of aging, not biological age point estimate


Epigenetic age acceleration = (biological age) − (chronological age)
Positive acceleration → aging faster → higher mortality, disease risk

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Computing Epigenetic Age

library(methylclock)

# Compute multiple epigenetic clocks at once
clocks <- DNAmAge(
  x        = beta,           # beta value matrix (probes × samples)
  clocks   = c("Horvath",
               "Hannum",
               "PhenoAge",
               "GrimAge"),
  cell.count = TRUE          # adjust for cell composition
)

# Age acceleration
clocks <- clocks |>
  mutate(
    AgeAccel_Horvath  = Horvath - age,
    AgeAccel_Hannum   = Hannum  - age,
    AgeAccel_PhenoAge = PhenoAge - age
  )

# Do cases age faster?
t.test(AgeAccel_GrimAge ~ Group, data = clocks)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
The Problem with Bulk RNA-seq
From last semester — bulk RNA-seq:
Tumor biopsy → homogenize → RNA → counts per gene

Gene X: 150 counts

But what does that mean?
Tumor cell A:    ████████  (high expression)
Tumor cell B:    ██        (medium)
Macrophage:      ████████  (high — confounding!)
Fibroblast:      ░░        (zero)
T cell:          ░░        (zero)

Bulk average: ████  ← misleading

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
What scRNA-seq Resolves

Every cell gets its own expression profile
Identify cell types without prior knowledge
Find rare cell populations (<1% of tissue)
Discover cell states within a cell type
Map gene expression heterogeneity within tumors
Connect to GWAS — in which cell type is the risk gene expressed?



scRNA-seq is now standard in Nature/Cell/Science papers.
As a clinician-scientist, you need to be able to interpret and run these analyses.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
How 10x Chromium Works
Single-cell suspension
    ↓
Microfluidic droplet formation
(one cell + one bead + oil → GEM)
    ↓
Cell barcoding + UMI tagging
    ↓
cDNA synthesis + amplification
    ↓
Library sequencing
    ↓

(cells × genes)

...

n_cells: 5,000–50,000
n_genes: ~20,000 (but 80–90% are zeros → sparse matrix)

The sparsity problem:
Each cell captures only ~5–15% of all transcripts → lots of zeros
This is a technical artifact (“dropout”) not true zero expression

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Overview
Cell Ranger output (barcodes, features, matrix)
    │
    ├── 1. Load & create Seurat object
    ├── 2. QC → filter low-quality cells
    ├── 3. Normalization → SCTransform
    ├── 4. Feature selection → highly variable genes
    ├── 5. Scaling & PCA
    ├── 6. Clustering → FindNeighbors + FindClusters
    ├── 7. UMAP visualization
    ├── 8. Marker gene identification
    └── 9. Cell type annotation → SingleR / manual

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 1: Load Data

library(Seurat)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Load 10x Cell Ranger output
counts <- Read10X(data.dir = here("data", "raw",
                                   "cellranger_output",
                                   "filtered_feature_bc_matrix"))

# Create Seurat object
seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts    = counts,
  project   = "PBMC",
  min.cells = 3,      # gene must be in ≥3 cells
  min.features = 200  # cell must have ≥200 genes
)

seurat
# 23,000 features × 8,000 samples (cells)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 2: QC — Three Key Metrics

# Mitochondrial gene percentage
seurat[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seurat,
                                                pattern = "^MT-")

# Ribosomal gene percentage
seurat[["percent.rb"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seurat,
                                                pattern = "^RP[SL]")

# Visualize
VlnPlot(seurat,
        features = c("nFeature_RNA",
                     "nCount_RNA",
                     "percent.mt"),
        ncol     = 3,
        pt.size  = 0)

# Scatter plot — doublets have high nCount + high nFeature
FeatureScatter(seurat, "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA",
               group.by = "orig.ident")

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
QC Thresholds

# Filter cells
seurat <- subset(seurat,
  nFeature_RNA > 200   &    # too few genes = dead cell
  nFeature_RNA < 5000  &    # too many genes = doublet
  nCount_RNA   < 25000 &    # too many UMIs  = doublet
  percent.mt   < 20)        # high MT% = damaged cell

cat("Cells before QC:", ncol(counts), "\n")
cat("Cells after QC: ", ncol(seurat), "\n")







Thresholds are dataset-specific


PBMC: MT% < 20% fine.
Cardiomyocytes: MT% up to 40% is normal (high mitochondrial content).
Always look at the distribution first, then set thresholds.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 3: Normalization — SCTransform

# SCTransform: regression-based normalization
# Accounts for sequencing depth differences between cells
seurat <- SCTransform(
  seurat,
  vars.to.regress = "percent.mt",   # regress out MT%
  verbose         = FALSE
)

# Result: "SCT" assay added to Seurat object
# Use SCT for all downstream analysis

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 4–6: PCA & Clustering

seurat <- RunPCA(seurat, verbose = FALSE)

# Elbow plot — how many PCs to use?
ElbowPlot(seurat, ndims = 50)

# Use top 30 PCs (adjust based on elbow plot)
seurat <- FindNeighbors(seurat, dims = 1:30, verbose = FALSE)
seurat <- FindClusters(seurat,
                        resolution = 0.5,   # higher = more clusters
                        verbose    = FALSE)

seurat <- RunUMAP(seurat, dims = 1:30, verbose = FALSE)

DimPlot(seurat, reduction = "umap",
        label = TRUE, pt.size = 0.5)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 7: Marker Genes per Cluster

# Find markers for each cluster vs. all other cells
all_markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  seurat,
  only.pos        = TRUE,    # only upregulated
  min.pct         = 0.25,    # expressed in ≥25% of cells
  logfc.threshold = 0.5,
  test.use        = "wilcox"
)

# Top 5 markers per cluster
top_markers <- all_markers |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 5)

# Heatmap of top markers
DoHeatmap(seurat,
          features = top_markers$gene,
          size     = 3) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Visualizing Marker Genes

# Feature plots — expression on UMAP
FeaturePlot(seurat,
            features = c("CD3E",    # T cells
                         "CD8A",    # CD8 T cells
                         "MS4A1",   # B cells
                         "CD14",    # Monocytes
                         "GNLY",    # NK cells
                         "PPBP"),   # Platelets
            ncol = 3,
            order = TRUE)

# Violin plots
VlnPlot(seurat,
        features = c("CD3E", "CD8A", "MS4A1"),
        ncol     = 3)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Manual vs. Automated Annotation
Manual: - Look at top marker genes per cluster - Check canonical markers (CD3E = T cell, CD14 = Monocyte…) - Time-consuming but gives full control
Automated — SingleR: - Compares each cell to reference transcriptomes - Fast, reproducible, reference-dependent - Best used as a starting point → manually validate

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
SingleR — Automated Annotation

library(SingleR)
library(celldex)

# Reference dataset — Human Primary Cell Atlas
hpca_ref <- HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData()

# Get normalized expression matrix
sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(seurat)

# Run SingleR
predictions <- SingleR(
  test      = sce,
  ref       = hpca_ref,
  labels    = hpca_ref$label.fine,
  assay.type.test = "logcounts"
)

# Add predictions to Seurat object
seurat$singler_labels <- predictions$labels

# Visualize
DimPlot(seurat, group.by = "singler_labels",
        label = TRUE, repel = TRUE) +
  NoLegend()

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Doublet Detection

library(DoubletFinder)

# Doublets = two cells captured in one droplet
# Look like cells with very high nFeature_RNA
# Must be removed before analysis

# Step 1: parameter sweep
sweep_res <- paramSweep_v3(seurat, PCs = 1:30,
                            sct = TRUE)
sweep_stats <- summarizeSweep(sweep_res, GT = FALSE)
bcmvn     <- find.pK(sweep_stats)
pK_val    <- as.numeric(as.character(
  bcmvn$pK[which.max(bcmvn$BCmetric)]))

# Step 2: run DoubletFinder
seurat <- doubletFinder_v3(
  seurat,
  PCs          = 1:30,
  pN           = 0.25,
  pK           = pK_val,
  nExp         = round(0.075 * ncol(seurat)),  # 7.5% expected
  reuse.pANN   = FALSE,
  sct          = TRUE
)

# Remove doublets
seurat <- subset(seurat, DF.classifications == "Singlet")

text:
Finalizing Annotations

# Add manual annotations based on marker genes + SingleR
cell_type_map <- c(
  "0" = "CD4 T cell",
  "1" = "CD8 T cell",
  "2" = "B cell",
  "3" = "Classical Monocyte",
  "4" = "NK cell",
  "5" = "Non-classical Monocyte",
  "6" = "Dendritic cell",
  "7" = "Platelet"
)

seurat$cell_type <- recode(as.character(seurat$seurat_clusters),
                            !!!cell_type_map)

# Final UMAP
DimPlot(seurat, group.by = "cell_type",
        label = TRUE, repel = TRUE,
        label.size = 4) +
  ggtitle("PBMC — Cell type annotation") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Pseudobulk — The Right Way

library(DESeq2)

# Wrong: treat each cell as independent observation → inflated p-values
# Right: aggregate cells per sample → pseudobulk → DESeq2

# Aggregate counts per cell type per sample
pseudobulk <- AggregateExpression(
  seurat,
  group.by     = c("cell_type", "sample_id"),
  assays       = "RNA",
  return.seurat = FALSE
)

# For each cell type, run DESeq2
run_pseudobulk_de <- function(cell_type_name, seurat_obj) {
  cells <- subset(seurat_obj, cell_type == cell_type_name)

  bulk  <- AggregateExpression(cells,
                                group.by   = "sample_id",
                                assays     = "RNA")$RNA

  meta  <- cells@meta.data |>
    distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id")

  dds   <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(bulk, meta, ~ condition)
  dds   <- DESeq(dds)
  results(dds)
}

de_cd8 <- run_pseudobulk_de("CD8 T cell", seurat)

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Why Visualization Matters

A great analysis with bad figures doesn’t get published
A mediocre analysis with compelling figures gets attention
Reviewers form first impressions from Figure 1 before reading methods
For your capstone: your hypothesis lives or dies by how clearly you present it



The figure is the argument. The methods section just explains how you got there.

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Five Principles

One message per panel — don’t overload a single plot
Direct labeling over legends — reduce eye travel
Color encodes meaning — don’t use color just to be colorful
Whitespace is not wasted — clutter kills clarity
Think about the reader’s path — A → B → C

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Grammar of Graphics Mindset

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Everything in ggplot2 is a layer
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +          # data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                    # geometry
  stat_smooth(method = "lm") +      # statistical transformation
  scale_color_manual(...) +         # scale
  facet_wrap(~ group) +             # facet
  labs(title = "...", x = "...") +  # labels
  theme_minimal()                    # theme








Build plots incrementally


Start with ggplot(data, aes()) + geom_point().
Add one layer at a time. Print after each addition.
Never write a 20-line ggplot in one go without checking.

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Volcano Plot — Publication Ready

library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Assume: de_results from DESeq2
de_results <- de_results |>
  mutate(
    status = case_when(
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange >  1 ~ "Up",
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Down",
      TRUE                               ~ "NS"
    ),
    label = ifelse(padj < 1e-10 | abs(log2FoldChange) > 3,
                   gene, NA)
  )

ggplot(de_results, aes(x = log2FoldChange,
                        y = -log10(padj),
                        color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label),
                   size     = 3,
                   max.overlaps = 20,
                   box.padding  = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Up   = "#D85A30",
                                 Down = "#185FA5",
                                 NS   = "gray70")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  labs(x     = "log₂ fold change",
       y     = "-log₁₀(adjusted p-value)",
       color = "",
       title = "Differential expression — Case vs. Control") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

                       c("#185FA5", "white", "#D85A30"))

  Group    = sample_metadata$group,
  Age      = sample_metadata$age,
  col      = list(
    Group = c(Control = "#1D9E75", Case = "#D85A30"),
    Age   = colorRamp2(c(20, 80), c("white", "#534AB7"))
  ),
  annotation_name_side = "left"
)

# Main heatmap
ht <- Heatmap(
  scaled_matrix,
  name                    = "z-score",
  col                     = col_fun,
  top_annotation          = ha,
  show_column_names       = FALSE,
  clustering_distance_rows = "pearson",
  clustering_method_rows  = "ward.D2",
  row_names_gp            = gpar(fontsize = 8),
  border                  = TRUE,
  row_title               = "Top DE genes"
)

draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right")

Panel Layout Principles

# Journal column widths:
# Single column: 3.5 inches
# 1.5 column:    5 inches
# Double column: 7 inches

  filename = here("results", "figures", "fig2.pdf"),
  plot     = my_figure,

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Axis Trap

# BAD: truncated y-axis exaggerates differences
ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 102))   # NEVER do this

# GOOD: start from 0 for bar charts
ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  expand_limits(y = 0)

# Exception: show variation when absolute value is less important
# (e.g., gene expression changes) → boxplot / violinplot, not bar
ggplot(data, aes(group, expression)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.5)

text:
Statistical Annotation

library(ggpubr)
library(rstatix)

# Compute statistics
stat_test <- data |>
  t_test(expression ~ group) |>
  add_significance() |>
  add_xy_position(x = "group")

# Add to plot
ggplot(data, aes(group, expression, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  stat_pvalue_manual(stat_test,
                     label     = "p.adj.signif",
                     tip.length = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1D9E75", "#D85A30")) +
  labs(y = "Expression (normalized)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Sample sizes — always, for every group
Statistical tests — name the test, not just “p < 0.05”

Effect sizes — OR, HR, log2FC — not just p-values
Software versions — R version + package versions (sessionInfo())
Data availability — GEO accession numbers, GitHub code repository
Reproducibility — seeds set, renv snapshot included

text:
Know your trait before you run anything
Genetic architecture = the landscape of genetic contributions: how many variants, how large their effects, how frequent they are, and how they interact [Timpson 2017].









Architecture
Variants
Example
Tools

The omnigenic model: regulatory networks are so interconnected that nearly every expressed gene exerts a tiny “peripheral” effect, funnelled through fewer “core” genes — this is why PRS (W3) works.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Allele frequency × effect size
Common variants tend to have small effects; large-effect variants tend to be rare (purifying selection removes common, large-effect, deleterious variants) [Timpson 2017].
 effect │ rare, large effect
  size  │  •           (Mendelian-like)
        │     • •
        │        • • •
        │             • • • • •   common, small effect
        │                       • • • • •  (typical GWAS hits)
        └──────────────────────────────────── MAF


Sample size is destiny — schizophrenia: ~0 hits at n≈hundreds, 113 loci at n in tens of thousands
Effect size ≠ druggability — common HMGCR SNP explains ~0.26% of LDL variance, yet statins are transformative








Important



Architecture can’t be predicted from heritability alone. Choose your study design after you understand the likely architecture.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Population stratification


If cases & controls differ in ancestry, any ancestry-associated variant looks like a disease hit.
▶️ Fix: PCA on genotypes → include top PCs as covariates so ancestry is absorbed by the model.

glm(disease ~ SNP +
      PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 +  # ancestry
      age + sex + batch,             # nuisance
    family = binomial)








ImportantAlways report ancestry — and its trade-off



Mixing populations uncorrected → false positives. Restricting to one ancestry → cleaner stats but limited generalizability (see Diversity).

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Why the threshold is 5×10⁻⁸


~1 million independent common-variant tests after LD pruning
Bonferroni: 0.05 / 1,000,000 = 5×10⁻⁸ → genome-wide significant
p < 1×10⁻⁵ → conventional suggestive line








Note



This is calibrated for common SNPs. Rare-variant and structural-variant tests (see Beyond SNPs) need their own thresholds.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
QQ plot & genomic inflation (λ)

qq(gwas_results$P, main = "QQ — observed vs expected −log10(p)")

chisq  <- qchisq(gwas_results$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Genomic inflation λ =", round(lambda, 3), "\n")



Well-calibrated: hug the diagonal, lift off at the tail (true signal)
Inflated (λ > 1.05): all above diagonal → uncorrected stratification / relatedness
Deflated (λ < 0.95): over-conservative QC → lost power
At very large n, modest λ can be genuine polygenicity — LD-score regression separates the two

Two examples worth remembering


UGT2B17 deletion → prostate cancer — alters testosterone metabolism; frequency varies by population → population-specific risk, invisible to SNP-only analysis [Harris 2025]
CYP2D6 copy number → drug dosing — deletions vs duplications shift codeine→morphine conversion (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers). Pharmacogenetics: the variant changes the right dose








NoteDosage sensitivity & “human knockouts”



Sequencing enables base-pair CNV calling at biobank scale. Aggregating loss-of-function variants (gnomAD LOEUF) builds dosage-sensitivity maps flagging genes intolerant to disruption — directly useful for clinical variant interpretation.

section: A hit is rarely the cause
text:
A hit is rarely the cause
A GWAS hit is usually a tag in LD with the real driver.
rs1234567  p = 3×10⁻²⁴            ← lead SNP (reported)
   ├── rs1234568  r² = 0.98
   ├── rs1234591  r² = 0.95       ← one (or more) is causal
   └── rs1234612  r² = 0.91
   (inherited together in a haplotype block)
Post-GWAS pipeline: 1) Fine-mapping → 2) Functional annotation → 3) Variant→gene → 4) Causal inference

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 0 — Linkage disequilibrium
LD both enables GWAS (one tag stands in for many) and complicates it (can’t tell tag from cause by p alone).

library(LDlinkR)

ld_matrix <- LDmatrix(
  snps  = c("rs1234567", "rs1234568", "rs1234591"),
  pop   = "CEU",            # 1000 Genomes population
  r2d   = "r2",
  token = "your_token"      # free at ldlink.nci.nih.gov
)

LDproxy(snp = "rs1234567", pop = "CEU", r2d = "r2", token = "your_token")







Warning



The LD reference panel must match your sample’s ancestry — a CEU panel on an East Asian cohort corrupts fine-mapping [Schaid 2018].

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 1 — Fine-mapping
Modern fine-mapping is Bayesian: compute a posterior inclusion probability (PIP) per variant, then a credible set — the smallest set containing the causal variant(s) with (e.g.) 95% probability [Schaid 2018].

library(susieR)

# SuSiE = Sum of Single Effects — allows multiple causal signals
susie_fit <- susie(X = genotype_matrix, y = phenotype_vector, L = 10)

cs  <- susie_get_cs(susie_fit, coverage = 0.95)  # 95% credible set(s)
pip <- susie_get_pip(susie_fit)                  # per-variant PIP







Note



Fine-mapping shrinks ~200 correlated SNPs to a credible set of a handful — if the data allow it.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
What controls fine-mapping resolution
Expected PIP rises with λ = N·R²/(1−R²) and falls as nearby SNPs get more correlated [Schaid 2018]:


Larger N → tighter credible sets (cheapest win)
High LD (ρ→1) → causal variants statistically indistinguishable in one sample
Functional annotation as a prior → modest help (90% set ~17.5 → ~13.5 SNPs for lipids); matters most in weak, high-LD regions









TipRobustness checklist




PIPs spread across many SNPs? → you likely can’t resolve one variant here
LD reference matches the sample? (compare allele frequencies)
Do SuSiE / FINEMAP / PAINTOR agree?
Multi-ancestry: assume shared causal variants, allow different effect sizes

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 2 — Functional annotation



Location
Likely mechanism




Coding (missense/nonsense)
direct protein change


Splice site
altered mRNA / isoform


Promoter / 5′UTR
transcription regulation


Enhancer
distal gene regulation


Intergenic / intronic
unknown — needs eQTL / chromatin









Important



~90% of GWAS hits are non-coding, enriched in regulatory elements and eQTLs — which is exactly why epigenomics (W4–W5) is essential for interpretation.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 3 — Variant → gene: colocalization
An eQTL affects a gene’s expression. Colocalization tests whether the GWAS and eQTL signals share the same causal variant.

library(coloc)

coloc_result <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_pvals, N = 150000, type = "cc", s = 0.3),
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_pvals, N = 500,    type = "quant")
)
coloc_result$summary   # PP.H4 = share one causal variant







Tip



PP.H4 > 0.8 → strong evidence the variant acts through that gene → strong effector candidate.








WarningWatch direction of effect (coherence)



A risk allele can down-regulate a gene that looks up-regulated in patients (“incoherence”) — often an impaired protective response. Direction decides agonist vs antagonist [Reay & Cairns 2021].

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 3 (cont.) — which cell type?
Colocalization names a gene; it doesn’t say which cell. Frameworks like sc-linker integrate scRNA-seq with GWAS via stratified LD-score regression (S-LDSC) [Minton 2022]:


Recovered known biology (T cells in eczema; microglia in Alzheimer’s & MS)
Surfaced candidates (GABAergic neurons in depression — current drugs target serotonin)
Separated disease-state programmes (M cells in ulcerative colitis) from healthy-state



A locus needs both a gene (coloc) and a cell type/state (single-cell) before you claim a mechanism.

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Step 4 — Mendelian randomization

Does elevated LDL cause CAD, or just correlate?

Variants = instruments; randomized at conception → mimic a lifelong RCT, immune to lifestyle/SES confounding.
Genetic variants → LDL level → CAD
   (instrument)    (exposure)  (outcome)

library(TwoSampleMR)

exposure_dat <- extract_instruments("ieu-a-300")            # LDL
outcome_dat  <- extract_outcome_data(snps = exposure_dat$SNP,
                                     outcomes = "ieu-a-7")  # CAD
dat    <- harmonise_data(exposure_dat, outcome_dat)
result <- mr(dat)                                            # IVW + sensitivity







Warning



IV assumptions: (1) relevance, (2) independence of confounders, (3) exclusion restriction. #3 is broken by pleiotropy — always run MR-Egger / weighted median [Reay & Cairns 2021].

text:
Three genetic strategies for repurposing


Locus → target — Open Targets Genetics, Priority index, MAGMA, TWAS (FUSION, S-PrediXcan)
MR for target validation — cis-variants in a druggable gene as instrument (PCSK9, IL6R)
Direction of effect — decides agonist vs antagonist (ties back to coherence)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
One variant, many phenotypes
GWAS   : one disease  → scan all variants    → "which variants?"
PheWAS : one variant  → scan all phenotypes   → "what else does it do?"
Typically run over electronic health records (ICD/CPT codes as phenotypes) [Denny 2016].


Pleiotropy mapping — repurposing leads and predictable side-effects
EHR-scale — one biobank → thousands of tests at once
Pharmacogenomic PheWAS (“MedWAS”) — variant → drug response / adverse events (free-text extraction is the bottleneck)

title: W2 — GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Why diverse cohorts matter
Most GWAS (→ fine-mapping → PRS) are European-ancestry — a scientific and equity problem [Wojcik 2019].


Missed discovery — variants rare/absent in Europeans are invisible; multi-ethnic PAGE found new associations
Better fine-mapping — different LD patterns break haplotype blocks → smaller credible sets
Poor portability — effect sizes & risk scores don’t transfer → biased clinical use widens disparities








ImportantFor Korean cohorts



Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, TOPMed). Check your base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting an association, credible set, or PRS.

text:
Step 1 — QC on summary stats

gwas_clean <- gwas |>
  filter(!is.na(P), P > 0, P <= 1,
         FREQ > 0.01, FREQ < 0.99,   # common variants
         INFO > 0.8) |>              # imputation quality
  mutate(CHR = as.integer(CHR),
         neglogP = -log10(P))

   main = paste0("QQ — T2D GWAS  (λ = ", round(lambda, 3), ")"),
   col  = "#185FA5")

          chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",

  attributes = c("chromosome_name", "start_position",

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
For person i, sum the GWAS effect size \(\hat\beta_j\) × allele dosage \(G_{ij}\) over all variants j:
\[\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \hat\beta_j \, G_{ij}\]
Person A:
  rs1001  risk allele × 0.03
+ rs2045  risk allele × 0.02
+ rs8821  non-risk    × 0.00
+ ... (thousands–millions more)
─────────────────────────────────
= PRS 1.42  → top 20% of population → ~3× risk

Crucially, variants below genome-wide significance still carry real signal — PRS deliberately includes them [Reay & Cairns 2021].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
W2’s omnigenic model: thousands of variants each nudge the trait
Single hits capture a sliver of heritability; aggregation captures much more
PRS is the clinical pay-off of polygenicity — one saliva sample → lifetime genetic predisposition








Note



A PRS is a risk indicator, not a diagnosis. It shifts a probability; it does not determine an outcome.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Coronary artery disease — flags high-risk people for earlier statins
Breast cancer — stratifies risk beyond BRCA1/2; guides screening intensity
Type 2 diabetes — PRS + lifestyle → targeted prevention
Atrial fibrillation — predicts incident AF beyond clinical scores
Prostate / colorectal cancer — screening intensity









TipThe clinician’s question



PRS adds information on top of age, BMI, family history, biomarkers. The bar is always: does it change management?

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 1 — C+T (clumping + thresholding)
The simplest, most interpretable approach:
1. Clump  : keep one SNP per LD block (independent signals)
2. Threshold : keep SNPs below a p-value cutoff (e.g. 5e-8, 0.05, ...)
3. Score  : PRS = Σ (effect size × allele dosage)

library(bigsnpr)

obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here::here("data", "raw", "target.rds"))
G <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes

ind.keep <- snp_clumping(
  G,
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  S         = abs(sumstats$beta / sumstats$beta_se),  # rank by |Z|
  thr.r2    = 0.1,
  size      = 500
)







Warning



The p-value threshold is arbitrary — C+T discards sub-threshold signal and needs tuning on a validation set.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 2 — LDpred2 (Bayesian, current standard)
Models LD explicitly and reweights all variants (no hard cutoff) under a Bayesian prior [Reay & Cairns 2021].

# 1) Match summary stats to target
sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, obj.bigsnp$map)

# 2) LD reference (genetic positions → correlation matrix)
POS2 <- snp_asGeneticPos(obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
                         obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
                         dir = here::here("data", "raw", "genetic_maps"))
corr <- snp_cor(G, ind.col = sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`,
                infos.pos = POS2, size = 3 / 1000)

# 3) Estimate h2, then LDpred2-auto (no validation set needed)
ldsc <- with(sumstats, snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                                chi2 = (beta / beta_se)^2, sample_size = n_eff))
multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(corr, sumstats, h2_init = ldsc[["h2"]],
                               vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, 30),
                               burn_in = 500, num_iter = 500)

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Choosing a method








Method
Pros
Cons




C+T
fast, interpretable
loses signal, arbitrary threshold


LDpred2
best accuracy, principled, -auto needs no tuning
slower, needs LD reference


PRSice2
easy, great plots
threshold-based


PRS-CS / PRS-CSx
continuous shrinkage; multi-ancestry
needs Python; LD panel




Clinical research: LDpred2 or PRSice2. Multi-ancestry: PRS-CSx. Consider a composite of several methods to reduce single-method assumptions [Kullo 2025].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Incremental variance (Nagelkerke R²)
Always report PRS performance above a clinical baseline — never PRS alone.

library(tidyverse); library(DescTools)

prs_data <- read_tsv(here::here("results", "prsice_output.best")) |>
  left_join(phenotype, by = "IID")

null_model <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)
full_model <- glm(disease ~ PRS + age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)

r2_prs <- PseudoR2(full_model, "Nagelkerke") -
          PseudoR2(null_model, "Nagelkerke")
cat("Incremental R² from PRS:", round(r2_prs, 4), "\n")

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Discrimination (AUC)

library(pROC)

roc_null <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(null_model, type = "response"))
roc_full <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(full_model, type = "response"))

roc.test(roc_null, roc_full)   # does PRS add discrimination?

ggroc(list(Clinical = roc_null, `Clinical + PRS` = roc_full)) +
  labs(title = "Does PRS improve prediction?", color = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()







Note



A statistically significant AUC bump can still be clinically trivial. Pair AUC with reclassification (NRI) and, above all, calibration.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Calibration — the underappreciated metric
Calibration = do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? [Kullo 2025]


Of people told “10% 10-year risk”, do ~10% develop disease?
A PRS well-calibrated in one population can be miscalibrated in another (different baseline risk, covariate distributions)
Fix by recalibration (update baseline hazard / intercept); assess in independent, population-representative cohorts








Important



Good discrimination ≠ good calibration. A model can rank people correctly yet output systematically wrong probabilities.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Quantile plot — the clinical view

prs_data <- prs_data |> mutate(prs_decile = ntile(PRS, 10))

or_by_decile <- prs_data |>
  group_by(prs_decile) |>
  summarise(n_cases = sum(disease == 1),
            n_ctrl  = sum(disease == 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(odds = n_cases / n_ctrl,
         OR   = odds / odds[prs_decile == 5])   # vs middle decile

ggplot(or_by_decile, aes(prs_decile, OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "PRS decile", y = "OR vs middle decile",
       title = "Disease risk by PRS decile") +
  theme_minimal()

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Same disease, different PRS → different person flagged
text:
Same disease, different PRS → different person flagged


Two PRSs with similar population AUC can disagree on which individual is high-risk [Kullo 2025]
Mitigations: consensus thresholds (high-risk only if top-tier across ≥2 scores) or a composite score
Risk also changes over time (age, comorbidity, exposures) → re-score with up-to-date methods; keep raw genotypes

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Four questions before the clinic (ACCE)
The 2025 review frames PRS readiness with the ACCE framework [Kullo 2025]:


Analytical validity — does the assay/pipeline measure the score accurately & reproducibly?
Clinical validity — does the score actually associate with the disease in the target population?
Clinical utility — does using it improve outcomes?
Ethical, legal, social implications — equity, consent, insurance, communication



Most PRSs clear analytical and clinical validity; the bottleneck is utility and ELSI.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Evidence for clinical utility is still thin
text:
Evidence for clinical utility is still thin
Few completed RCTs [Kullo 2025]:


MI-GENES (CHD) — PRS-integrated risk → lower LDL at 6 mo, fewer events at 10 yr (earlier/longer statin use)
GenoVA — PRS for 6 diseases (CHD, T2D, AF, breast/colorectal/prostate cancer): effect on time-to-diagnosis
WISDOM / PERSPECTIVE — PRS-guided mammography intensity
eMERGE (US, 10 conditions) and Our Future Health (UK, 5M) — implementation at scale








Note



RCTs are slow and costly — cohort, health-economics, simulation and implementation-science studies all contribute evidence.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Communicating risk: three framings
A percentile alone is not enough — it doesn’t say how much disease risk it explains [Kullo 2025].








Framing
Example
Caveat




Absolute risk
“18% over 10 years”
needs incidence data (often missing)


Relative risk / OR
“2.3× population average”
no baseline anchor


Percentile rank
“top 5% of PRS”
says nothing about absolute magnitude




Absolute risk linked to a guideline action is the most clinically actionable framing.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Integrating PRS into existing risk equations
text:
Integrating PRS into existing risk equations


Breast cancer — BOADICEA: the one clinical equation combining PRS + family history + rare variants + clinical factors
CHD — Pooled Cohort Equations: PRS is ~orthogonal → add log-additively
Most other diseases: no validated absolute-risk equation yet → estimate from epidemiological incidence
Lifetime risk can vary dramatically by PRS centile — e.g. ER-positive breast cancer ~2% to ~31% bottom vs top centile

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
The human barriers


Patients hold deterministic views of genetics; risk is actually probabilistic and modifiable (MI-GENES framed it as mutable)
Run many PRSs at once → most people flagged high-risk for something → alarm fatigue
Primary-care providers often lack genomics training → need CDS tools, a trained “champion user”, and PRS in medical curricula

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Why the EHR changes the game
text:
Why the EHR changes the game
Biobanks now link genotypes to EHRs at population scale, so PRS can be built and applied without a bespoke study [Li 2020].


Khera et al. 2018: a PRS can flag people with risk equivalent to a monogenic mutation (CAD, AF, T2D, IBD, breast cancer)
Rich phenotypes: diagnoses, labs, imaging, meds — plus easy, well-defined controls
Examples: Michigan Genomics Initiative, UK Biobank, National Biobank of Korea, Biobank Japan, China Kadoorie

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Turning an EHR into phenotypes


ICD codes — first-line case/control definitions (but coding practices differ between systems)
NLP on clinical notes — extract phenotypes from free text
PheKB — 50+ portable phenotyping algorithms with high positive predictive value








WarningEHR data is messy




Sparse & irregular — sicker patients have richer records (Geisinger: only 20/143 variables had <25% missingness)
Medication adherence not captured — prescribed ≠ taken
Phenotyping errors propagate into PRS evaluation

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Infrastructure for clinical PRS
A workable pipeline needs more than a model [Kullo 2025]:


PGS Catalog — open repository of published scores (alleles + weights + metadata)
FHIR — standard for moving genomic + clinical data between systems
TRE / cloud — compute PRS on-demand with QC’d pipelines
CDS + EHR dashboard — show PRS alongside family history, smoking, labs
Metadata — record algorithm version + ancestry-specific performance for traceability

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Genetic correlation — how much do two diseases share?
text:
Genetic correlation — how much do two diseases share?
Genetic correlation (r_g) quantifies the overlap in heritable basis between two traits [van Rheenen 2019].


Bivariate LDSC — estimates r_g straight from summary statistics, robust to sample overlap (LD Hub hosts hundreds of traits)
Bivariate GREML — from individual genotypes
e.g. schizophrenia ↔︎ bipolar disorder r_g ≈ 0.6



A high r_g explains comorbidity and shared biology, and predicts cross-disorder risk in relatives — directly relevant when counselling families.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Why clinicians should care about r_g
text:
Why clinicians should care about r_g


Comorbidity — shared genetics anticipates co-occurring diagnoses
Borrowing power — pleiotropy-informed methods (MTAG) boost a small GWAS using a correlated, larger one
Cross-disorder risk — a relative’s risk depends on r_g, kinship, heritability and prevalence








Warning



r_g estimates can be distorted by assortative mating, misclassification, collider bias and stratification — interpret with the same care as MR [van Rheenen 2019].

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: PRS does not transfer across ancestries
text:
PRS does not transfer across ancestries


Most GWAS (→ PRS) are European-ancestry
A European-trained PRS performs ~4–5× worse in African-ancestry individuals [Martin, in Li 2020]
Roots: different allele frequencies, LD, and effect sizes from distinct population history (drift, selection, bottlenecks) [Kullo 2025]
Deploying biased PRS clinically can widen health disparities

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
What to do about it


Prefer ancestry-matched base GWAS; use PRS-CSx / multi-ancestry meta-analysis
Report ancestry-specific performance and recalibrate per population
Invest in diverse cohorts — diversity also sharpens fine-mapping (W2)








ImportantFor Korean patients



Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, National Biobank of Korea, TOPMed). Always check the base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting a PRS.

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Honest limitations


Not causal — high PRS ≠ will develop disease
Misses rare, high-penetrance variants — BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome need dedicated testing
Misses non-SNP variation — CNV/SV/repeats (W2 §Beyond SNPs)
Gene × environment — genetic risk is modifiable by lifestyle/medication
Not a diagnosis — one input among many, not a verdict
Dynamic — risk and methods both change over time

title: W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Key takeaways


PRS turns polygenicity into one actionable number — but it’s a risk indicator, not a diagnosis
Always evaluate incremental value, and don’t forget calibration
Clinical readiness = ACCE, not just AUC; utility evidence is still emerging
The hard parts are portability, communication, and EHR integration — not the maths
